'''Michel Matthew Ter-Pogossian''' (April 21, 1925{{spaced ndash}}June 19, 1996) was an Armenian-American [[medical physicist]].<ref name="jama"/> He was professor of [[radiology]] at the [[Washington University School of Medicine]] for over 30 years. A pioneer in [[nuclear medicine]],<ref name="Kanno"/> he is best known for his research on the [[positron emission tomography]] (PET). He is considered one of its creators and often referred to as the "father of PET."<ref name="Rich"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Michel Ter-Pogossian (1925-96) |url=http://broughttolife.sciencemuseum.org.uk/broughttolife/people/michelterpogossian |publisher=[[Science Museum, London]] |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20200103202315/http://broughttolife.sciencemuseum.org.uk/broughttolife/people/michelterpogossian |archivedate=3 January 2020 |quote=He became widely known as the ‘father of PET’.}}</ref>

==Early life==
Ter-Pogossian was born on April 21, 1925, in [[Berlin]] to [[Armenians|Armenian]] parents from the [[Ottoman Empire]] who escaped the [[Armenian genocide]].<ref name="Wackers"/><ref name="nytobit"/> He was the only child.<ref name="wustl bio"/> His family later moved to France, where Ter-Pogossian grew up.<ref name="wustl bio"/><ref name="Wackers"/> He developed an early interest in science and experimented with toy physics and chemistry kits as a child.<ref name="wustl bio"/><ref name="nytobit"/><ref name="Wackers"/> Ter-Pogossian attended the [[University of Paris]], from which he received his bachelor's degree in mathematics<ref name="JNucMed"/> in 1942<ref name="jama"/><ref name="Wackers"/><ref name="nytobit"/> or 1943.<ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="wustl bio"/> He subsequently studied at the [[Curie Institute (Paris)|Institute of Radium]] under [[Irène Joliot-Curie]], graduating in 1946.<ref name="jama"/><ref name="wustl bio"/><ref name="PhysToday"/> He was active in the [[French Resistance]] during World War II.<ref name="Wackers"/><ref name="nytobit"/>

==Career==
Ter-Pogossian moved to the United States in 1946 to complete his studies.<ref name="wustl bio"/><ref name="nytobit"/> He preferred the U.S. over Britain because the former seemed "more exciting."<ref name="Wackers"/><ref name="nytobit"/> He enrolled at [[Washington University in St. Louis]] as a graduate student in 1946.<ref name="PhysToday"/> He was drawn to the university by and studied under [[Arthur Compton]], who was also the university's chancellor at the time.<ref name="jama"/><ref name="wustl bio"/> He simultaneously worked in the physics department as a [[research assistant]].<ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="wustl bio"/> Ter-Pogossian received his master's degree in 1948,<ref name="wustl bio"/> and his Ph.D. in [[nuclear physics]] from WashU in 1950.<ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="jama"/>

He joined the [[Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology]] at WashU in 1950.<ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="wustl bio"/><ref name="the-scientist"/> In the same year he also joined the faculty of [[Washington University School of Medicine]] as an instructor in radiation physics.<ref name="Wackers"/><ref name="Vannier"/> He was named professor of radiation physics in 1961, professor of biophysics in physiology in 1964, and professor of radiation sciences in 1973.<ref name="Vannier"/><ref name="Wackers"/>

Between 1963 and 1991 Ter-Pogossian served as director of the division of radiation sciences at the Mallinckrodt Institute.<ref name="Vannier"/><ref name="Wackers"/><ref name="nytobit"/>{{efn|Other sources indicate 1973 as the year he became head of the Division of Radiation Sciences.<ref name="wustl bio"/><ref name="PhysToday"/>}} After resigning from administrative duties in 1990, Ter-Pogossian devoted all his time to research.<ref name="Wackers"/> He was a self-proclaimed "research junkie".<ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="nytobit"/> He became emeritus professor in 1995.<ref name="Vannier"/><ref name="Wackers"/><ref name="wustl bio"/>

==Work==
Ter-Pogossian spent his entire professional career at Washington University's Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology.<ref name="jama"/> His research focused on "increasing the number of practical clinical applications of cerebral scanning."<ref name="the-scientist"/> His work resulted in improvement of [[medical imaging]], [[radiation therapy]], and [[brachytherapy]]. He developed a new type of nuclear medicine [[gamma camera]], known as the "Ter-Pogossian camera."<ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="jama"/>

In 1951 Ter-Pogossian developed a pioneering scanner that detected radioactivity concentrations in living material.<ref name="JNucMed"/><ref name="nytobit"/> In the mid-1950s he "reported the first biomedical application of a sodium iodide detector for the diagnosis and localization of intracranial tumors."<ref name="JNucMed"/>

===Positron emission tomography (PET)===
Ter-Pogossian was a pioneer in the use of cyclotron-produced [[radioactive tracer]]s.<ref name="Wackers"/> He is best known for his work on the [[positron emission tomography]] (PET). His research began in the 1950s with a series of experiments that made PET a "practical diagnostic tool"<ref name="jama"/> by the 1970s.<ref name="JNucMed"/><ref name="nytobit"/>

His early work led to the installation of a small biomedical cyclotron in the basement at the [[Washington University Medical Center]] in 1963.<ref name="JNucMed"/> He persuaded several government agencies to support the research.<ref name="jama"/> It was the first cyclotron in the U.S. located in a medical center.<ref name="JNucMed"/> The cyclotron produced short-lived, [[Positron emission|positron-emitting]] [[radionuclide]]s intended to be used to develop techniques for measuring regional cerebral blood flow, oxygen metabolism, blood volume, and glucose metabolism.<ref name="JNucMed"/> The first PET unit was created in 1974 by the group led by Ter-Pogossian.<ref name="JNucMed"/> A decade later, PET units of that design were "used in many medical centers throughout the world."<ref name="JNucMed"/>

Ter-Pogossian is recognized to have "led the research that turned the positron emission tomography (PET) scanner from an intriguing concept to a medical tool used in hospitals and laboratories everywhere."<ref name="nytobit"/> With [[Edward J. Hoffman]] and [[Michael E. Phelps]] "he played a major role turning positron imaging from a laboratory concept into practical imaging protocols and devices that are currently used worldwide."<ref name="Wackers"/>

==Personal life and death==
Ter-Pogossian married visual artist [[Ann Ter-Pogossian|Ann Dodson (née Scott)]], of [[St. Louis]], in 1966.<ref name="family">{{cite web |title=Ann Garrison Scott Dodson Ter-Pogossian |url=https://www.familysearch.org/tree/person/sources/G666-2QF |website=Family Search |publisher=The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints |access-date=24 December 2022}}</ref> Ann (1932–2022)<ref name="family"/> had a master's degree in [[Egyptology]] and participated in exhibitions from 1973 to 2003, including the prestigious [[Florence Biennale]].<ref name="artnet">{{cite web |title=Ann Ter-Pogossian Biography |url=https://www.artnet.com/artists/ann-ter-pogossian/biography |website=Artnet |publisher=Artnet Worldwide Corporation |access-date=24 December 2022}}</ref> After her marriage to Michel, she signed her work and exhibited under the name Ann Ter-Pogossian. Ann had two sons and a daughter by her first marriage.<ref name="family"/><ref name="jama"/><ref name="nytobit"/> The Ter-Pogossians were residents of [[Clayton, Missouri]].<ref name="wapo"/> 

Ter-Pogossian was described by Ronald G. Evens as a "citizen of the world."<ref name="jama"/> He traveled extensively and was a [[gourmet]] and a [[scuba diver]].<ref name="PhysToday"/> He died on June 19, 1996, of apparent [[myocardial infarction]] in Paris, while on a vacation.<ref name="nytobit"/><ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="jama"/><ref name="Wackers"/>

==Recognition==
Ter-Pogossian was an "internationally known pioneer in the use of cyclotron-produced radionuclides in biomedical research."<ref name="PhysToday"/> [[Frans Wackers]] noted that he is "widely recognized as one of the fathers of PET imaging."<ref name="Wackers"/> He has been called "the father of PET" by some.<ref name="Rich"/><ref name="jama"/><ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="wustl bio"/> Ter-Pogossian emphasized that PET is the product of teamwork and elaborated:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dumit |first1=Joseph |authorlink1=Joseph Dumit |title=Picturing Personhood: Brain Scans and Biomedical Identity |date=2004 |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |isbn=9780691113982 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=FOk9DwAAQBAJ&dq=Ter-Pogossian&pg=PA41 41-44]}}</ref>
{{quote frame|...when somebody referred to me as the father of PET, I said, "I'd rather be the mother of PET, because many offspring have many fathers, and only one mother. As a matter of fact, some offspring have no father at all!" Of course there are many fathers. [...] [it's obvious that] there are masses of fathers of PET. Again, the important point is—I'm not suggesting that to you; it is probably obvious—is again the convergence of so many different disciplines. The development of the scintillation counter, artificial radioactivity, and so on.}}

===Awards===
*Paul C. Aebersold Award, [[Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging]] (1976)<ref>{{cite web |title=Paul C. Aebersold Award Recipients |url=http://snmmi.files.cms-plus.com/docs/Grants_and_Awards/Paul_Aebersold_Awardee_List.pdf |publisher=[[Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging]] |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20200105131058/http://snmmi.files.cms-plus.com/docs/Grants_and_Awards/Paul_Aebersold_Awardee_List.pdf |archivedate=5 January 2020 |quote=1976 Michael M. Ter-Pergossian, PhD}}</ref>
*Georg Charles de Hevesy Nuclear Medicine Pioneer Award, [[Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging]] (1985)<ref name="JNucMed"/>
*[[Canada Gairdner International Award]] (1993) "For contributions to the development and application of positron emission tomography"<ref>{{cite web |title=Michel M. Ter-Pogossian BA MS PHD |url=https://gairdner.org/award_winners/michel-m-ter-pogossian/ |website=gairdner.org |publisher=[[Gairdner Foundation]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211018224105/https://gairdner.org/award_winners/michel-m-ter-pogossian/ |archive-date=18 October 2021}}</ref><ref name="the-scientist"/>

===Membership===
Ter-Pogossian was a member of many professional societies: charter member of the [[American Nuclear Society]], fellow of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref name="wustl bio"/> honorary fellow of the [[American College of Radiology]],<ref name="JNucMed"/> [[National Academy of Medicine|Institute of Medicine]] (elected in 1987).<ref name="wustl bio"/>

He was a trustee of the [[Academy of Science, St. Louis]] and served as an adviser to several [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]], [[National Institutes of Health]] and [[Food and Drug Administration]] committees.<ref name="JNucMed"/><ref name="PhysToday"/><ref name="wustl bio"/> He served on the editorial boards of several journals, including the ''[[American Journal of Roentgenology]]'', the ''[[Journal of Nuclear Medicine]]'', and the ''Journal de Biophysique & Médecine Nucléaire''.<ref name="wustl bio"/><ref name="PhysToday"/> He was the first editor of the ''IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging'', published by the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]].<ref name="Vannier"/>
